passages.happening:
‘Then Josiah celebrated the Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem, and the Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month’ (verse 1). He sets the priests in their duties and tells the Levites, “Put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon son of David king of Israel. It is not to be carried around on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and His people Israel” (verse 3). They are to prepare by their families and divisions, as David and Solomon had written (verse 4).

Josiah gives thirty thousand lambs and goats and three thousand cattle from his own flocks for the people, and his officials give freely too (verses 7-9). The Levites slaughter and skin the animals, the priests sprinkle the blood, the lambs are roasted and the holy offerings boiled and shared, and the singers and gatekeepers stay at their posts while the Levites prepare for them (verses 10-15). ‘No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 34 renewed the covenant; this chapter shows it kept in worship. Josiah's Passover, in his eighteenth year, commonly dated 622 BC, is the high point of the reform and the last great festival in the story of the kings. Passover, pesach, named for the LORD's passing over the marked houses, was first a household meal and by Josiah's day a national feast at the central sanctuary. The Levites slaughtered and distributed the animals so families could eat, and the king and officials gave tens of thousands of animals so the poor could take part.

The verb prepare, kun, comes again and again: order and readiness, everything done according to Moses, David and the king's command. The command to put the ark in the temple is puzzling, since Solomon had placed it there. Some think it had been removed under Manasseh or during the repairs; others read the verse as saying that the Levites no longer needed to carry it and should turn to other duties. It is the last mention of the ark in the historical books.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You are not to sacrifice the Passover animal in any of the towns that the LORD your God is giving you’ (Deuteronomy 16:5), but at the place he would choose.
passages.asks: Josiah gave from his own flocks so that the poor could keep the feast. Ask who cannot afford to join in what you enjoy in worship and community. And ask what you could give so that they can.

passages.t: Neco, a disguise, and Josiah's death
passages.happening:
‘After all this, when Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco king of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish by the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to confront him’ (verse 20). Neco sends messengers: he has not come against Josiah, ‘God told me to hurry; so stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you’ (verse 21). ‘Josiah, however, did not turn away from him; instead, in order to engage him in battle, he disguised himself. He did not listen to Neco’s words from the mouth of God, but went to fight him on the Plain of Megiddo’ (verse 22).

Archers shoot Josiah, and he tells his servants he is badly wounded (verse 23). They bring him to Jerusalem, where he dies, ‘And Josiah was buried in the tomb of his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him’ (verse 24). Jeremiah laments over him, and the singers still sing laments over Josiah (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
With a single phrase, after all this, the tone changes. The king who listened so well to the book does not listen to a word from an unexpected mouth, and he dies in a battle he did not need to fight. Josiah died in 609 BC. Assyria had lost Nineveh and was making a last stand in northern Mesopotamia, and Pharaoh Neco the Second marched north to support it against rising Babylon. Josiah's motive is not stated; many historians think he hoped to prevent an Egyptian and Assyrian recovery that would threaten Judah's new freedom. Megiddo guarded a key pass on the road north, and its plain saw many battles. Carchemish, on the Euphrates, would be the site of Babylon's decisive victory over Egypt in 605 BC.

The death scene deliberately echoes Ahab's in chapter 18: a king disguises himself, goes to battle against a warning, is struck by archers and tells his men he is wounded. The disguise, chaphas, is the same verb. Josiah, the best of the later kings, dies in the manner of the north's most notorious king, because he did not listen to the words from the mouth of God. Laments, qun, for fallen kings were a recognized form; the Book of Laments named in verse 25 is lost, and it is not the biblical book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of Jerusalem.
passages.later: Second Kings tells it briefly: ‘King Josiah went out to confront him, but Neco faced him and killed him at Megiddo’ (2 Kings 23:29). Zechariah later spoke of a wailing ‘as great as the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo’ (Zechariah 12:11).
passages.hard:
Huldah promised that Josiah would go to his grave in peace. How does that fit his death in battle? And how could God speak through a pagan king?

Huldah's promise explained itself: Josiah's eyes would not see the calamity coming on Jerusalem. In that sense it was kept; he died before the Babylonian conquest and was buried in his fathers' tomb with national mourning. Many interpreters read peace in that light, as dying before the judgment and receiving honorable burial. Others see the promise as conditional on Josiah's continued obedience, and note that the Chronicler blames his death on his refusal to listen to God's word through Neco.

Chronicles presents God speaking through a foreign king as a plain fact, and the book's last verses will show God stirring another foreign king, Cyrus. Both explanations of the promise take the text seriously; the second fits the Chronicler's pattern of explaining a king's end by his response to God's word.
passages.asks: Josiah listened to the book and not to a warning from an unlikely source. Ask whom you would never expect God to speak through, and whether you have refused a true word because of who said it. And ask what battle you are going out to fight that is not yours.
